newsitem.title: UK: Copper ends at two-month LME peak above $2,000.
newsitem.headline: Copper ends at two-month LME peak above $2,000.

text.p: Copper prices surged during active Friday afternoon LME trading, ending at the highest for two months as the market finally broke out of the $1,900/70 range it has languished in all month.
Traders said breaking above $1,970 uncovered buy-stops, and as the pace of trading picked up heavy short-covering from one quarter in particular saw prices charge through $2,000 and then $2,020.
The gains were augmented by tightening spreads and fundamental concerns over stoppages in Chile and Africa.

"It was initially a technical move, with $1,970 obviously the key number. Above there the shorts had to cover with a holiday in New York, but these other factors (tightness and strikes) played a part as well," one said.

Chile's Salvador mine is strike-bound, as is Gold Fields Namibia Tsumeb smelter. Meanwhile, cash/threes moved out to $60 backwardation - double mid-week levels, as the key September prompt dates approached
Last business was at the high of $2,039 a tonne, an $80 gain from Thursday's kerb close.
Other metals were carried higher by copper, with volumes similarly picking up as prices broke out of stagnant narrow ranges.
The end of the summer slowdown and the approach of the traditionally busy final quarter should see more active physical intersest, traders said.
Aluminium cleared $1,500, and absorbed some late profit-taking to finish at $1,512 a tonne, up $15. The next target is $1,540, traders said.
Nickel's gains were trimmed in late trading, although the market still closed firmer, bolstered by the strike mandate at Inco's Manitoba facilities, ahead of the labour contract expiry next month.
Last business was at $7,490 a tonne, still $65 up from Thursday, with levels above $7,500 likely to be challenged again next week.

Lead and zinc also pulled back from their mid-afternoon highs, but remained steadier against a background of supply-side fundamentals. Lead is being helped by the Tsumeb stoppage, as there is a lead smelter there, while less zinc metal will be available during the remainder of the year from Noranda's Brunswick operations.
Last lead business was at $812, a $7.50 gain, while zinc finished at $1,033, up $4.50 from Thursday. Of the two metals, analysts see more gains in lead as supply/demand fundamentals are tighter.

Tin similarly slid back from its peaks above $6,300, but looks set to benefit from copper's new-found bull-run in the short-term, with levels of $6,500 being targetted. Last kerb trade was at $6,260, up $45.
The alloy contract was marked higher, ending at $1,304/1,305 a tonne.
